audio_caption: The clip begins with one male speaker describing the relationship between energy and mass, referencing the equation "E equals mc squared" and the idea that energy can create mass, noting the need for "twice the energy." He suggests exploring "pair production and annihilation." A distinct "wooosh" sound effect is heard between the speaker's sentences.

The clip begins with a man explaining that matter particles and their antimatter counterparts need to be produced, using the electron and positron as an example. He continues, discussing a cloud chamber, the water vapor saturation inside, and how charged particles leave tracks. He explains a magnetic field used to make moving charged particles move in circles, depending on their mass and charge, and how Carl Anderson found positive charges in cosmic rays. The speaker clarifies that the mass of the particles was at most twice the mass of an electron. In a quieter tone, he refers to a figure, from 1932, that shows a positron.

The audio clip begins with a male speaker discussing particle production, mentioning "better detectors" and "production on demand," as well as an example from the ALICE detector at CERN, specifically "pair production of electrons positrons." He describes the reaction that causes an electron-positron pair, noting the energy needed. Transitioning to a more technical explanation, he references the equation E=mc², relating mass to energy, and provides an example using a kilogram of mass, about "one liter of water." He then calculates the energy that would be produced, stating that the "speed of light is exactly 299 million 792,458 meters a second," and concludes that "we get nine followed by sixteen zeros joules of energy." He assesses that the numbers are "kind of meaningless without an example."

The audio clip starts with a male speaker introducing a topic, mentioning "Fat Man" and a bomb dropped on Nagasaki. He speaks in a conversational and informative tone, outlining calculations involving joules and liters of water. He then transitions to discussing "anti-water" and questioning the practical application of the equation E=mc^2. He maintains a thoughtful tone, proposing to clarify some aspects to better understand the concept.

The audio clip begins with one speaker, who seems to be male, explaining an equation and mass in relation to energy. He defines the new measure of energy, then transitions to discussing the mass of an electron, proton, neutron, and deuterium nucleus in megaelectronvolts. The tone is educational and informative.

The audio clip begins with a male speaker discussing the properties of deuterium, explaining that it's composed of a proton and neutron and exploring why it is lighter than its components. He maintains an informative tone, noting the differences in mass and introducing the concept of binding energy to explain the loss of mass as a loss of energy. The speaker uses terms such as "mass and energy are equivalent" and explains that when a system goes to a lower state, "the difference of energy has to come from somewhere". The content transitions into how separating deuterium requires energy and concluding that this process is the basis of how nuclear fusion and fission work.

The audio clip begins with a male speaker explaining nuclear fusion as the process of atoms and protons and neutrons binding together, giving the example of deuterium and helium nuclei. The speaker describes the amount of energy released during fusion and compares binding energy between lighter and heavier elements. He then talks about Uranium 238 fissioning into an alpha particle and Thorium 234. He switches topics and talks about the mass difference between a proton and a neutron, and describes the decay of a free neutron when it isn't caught up in an atom. He states that neutrons have a half-life of about 15 minutes and the probability that it will change into a proton. Another male speaker then clarifies that "the wave function of the neutron has changed into a superposition of both, each with a probability of half". The speakers appear to be speaking clearly and conversationally.

The audio begins with a male speaker concluding part one of a discussion. He announces the start of part two, mentioning that it will explain "nuclear fission." The audio solely features the voice of this one male speaker, presented in a conversational tone.
